hook.text: Once your words are clean, the next thing to do is count them.

fox.text: Take a short text about a fox and a dog. Without its punctuation, it's thirty words.

tally.text: NLTK's FreqDist, short for frequency distribution, tallies every one: thirteen different words, and the word the comes first, eight times.

common.text: Ask it for the five most common, and you get words with their counts, highest first.

ratio-in.text: And thirteen out of thirty says something too. This text repeats itself.

diversity.text: That ratio, different words over total words, is called lexical diversity.

very.text: Very, very, very good, good, good, good has two different words in seven. That's zero point two nine.

varied.text: A sentence that never repeats scores a perfect one.

length.text: But the score falls as a text grows, because common words keep coming back.

emma-length.text: The first hundred words of Jane Austen's Emma score zero point seven three. The first thousand, zero point four two. Ten thousand, zero point one eight. The whole novel, zero point oh four.

same.text: So only compare texts of the same length.

tail-in.text: And a whole novel shows something bigger: the shape of language.

book.text: Emma runs to a hundred and sixty-one thousand words, but only about seven thousand different ones.

giants.text: Rank them by count, and the top ten alone make up over a fifth of the book.

hapax.text: At the other end, more than two thousand seven hundred words appear just once. They're called hapaxes.

zipf.text: That's nearly two in five of the vocabulary. A few giants and a long, thin tail: it's called Zipf's law, and almost every text has it.

grows.text: And the tail never closes. Even Emma's last ten thousand words bring a hundred and eighty-eight it hadn't used before.

top-in.text: [curious] So what does the top of the list tell you about the book?

top.text: Emma's six most common words are to, the, and, of, I and a.

nothing.text: Not one of them says what the novel is about.

without.text: Drop the stopwords and count again: Mister, Emma, could, would, Missus, Miss.

heroine.text: Now the heroine's name comes second.

commonplace.text: Raw frequency rewards the commonplace. Filter first, and the topic comes through.

tag-in.text: But a count only sees spelling. It can't tell what job a word is doing.

fish.text: Take fish. In I caught a big fish, it's a noun. In we fish on weekends, it's a verb.

jobs.text: Same spelling, two jobs, and a counter can't tell them apart.

tagging.text: Part-of-speech tagging labels every word with its job, judged from the words around it.

tagger.text: NLTK's tagger learned from text that people tagged by hand. It calls the first fish NN, a noun, and the second VBP, a verb.

penn.text: Those labels come from the Penn Treebank, the hand-tagged text it learned from.

meanings.text: A determiner, an adjective, a noun, a present-tense verb for he, she or it, and a plural noun.

letters.text: There are about thirty-six, but the first letter does most of the work: N for nouns, V for verbs, J for adjectives, R for adverbs.

extract.text: That's enough to pull patterns out of text. Tag the talented young engineer quietly designed a brilliant new system, and keep the tags that start with N.

nouns.text: You get the nouns: engineer and system.

adjectives.text: J gives the adjectives, talented, young, brilliant and new. V gives designed, and R, quietly.

lemma.text: Tags fix lemmatizing, too. The WordNet lemmatizer treats every word as a noun, unless it's told otherwise.

untouched.text: So in the runners were running and they had eaten well, running and eaten come back untouched.

tagfirst.text: Tag first, hand each word its tag's first letter, and running becomes run, eaten becomes eat.

recipe.text: Tag, then lemmatize: that's the accurate recipe.

pairs-in.text: Still, every step so far looks at one word at a time.

together.text: But New York, machine learning and not good only mean something together.

ngram.text: An n-gram is n words in a row. Two make a bigram, three make a trigram.

slide.text: Slide a window two words wide along the quick brown fox jumps, one step at a time, so the windows overlap.

formula.text: Five words give four bigrams, and three trigrams:

compare.text: Why bother? Compare the food was good with the food was not good.

sets.text: As sets of single words, they differ by one word: not.

bigram.text: As bigrams, only one has not good. A lone not turns up in praise too, like not bad. The pair is what a sentiment model can learn is negative.

phrases.text: Counting bigrams finds phrases, too. In three short lines about machine learning, the top pair is machine learning, three times.

cast.text: Over all of Emma, keep the pairs with no stopword in them, and out walks the cast: Mister Knightley, Missus Weston, Mister Elton.

bigger-in.text: [curious] So if two words in a row help, would five help more?

sparse.text: Usually not. Take each n-gram in Emma, and ask: does it appear anywhere else?

shares.text: Single words almost always do. Bigrams, seven times in ten. Trigrams, about one in four. Four in a row, one in fifteen, and five, almost never.

sparsity.text: An n-gram seen only once tells you almost nothing: one sighting can't tell a pattern from an accident. That's sparsity.

sweet.text: So bigrams are the sweet spot, and trigrams with plenty of text: enough order to help, still common enough to count.

next.text: But a model wants numbers, not lists of words. So next, we'll turn text into features.

tall.text: The tall man reads books comes back as DT, JJ, NN, VBZ and NNS.

even.text: Even were and had become be and have.

rule.text: the number of words, minus n, plus one.
